name: Mono Essay
basis: video-essay frame: sunk monochrome, thin white contours, circle, rule and caption (how)
note: Grain and scratches are garnish, not a modelled film process.

lumenary.blurb: A frame from a quiet video essay: the picture sunk into grainy black and white, one thin white contour drawn round its forms, a circle, a rule and a single sentence set small and wide.

facts.from: Online video essays and minimalist editorial design
facts.bestOn: One clear subject against a plain background

why: A quiet essay video asks you to listen, so its pictures step back. Colour goes, the blacks deepen until most of the frame is dark, and grain makes a still image feel like film. Over that, a few thin white lines do the pointing: a contour around the forms, a circle, a rule, one short sentence. The picture becomes a diagram of an idea.
how: Reduce the picture to brightness and stretch it to the full range.
Sink it: a smoothstep sends everything below a limit to black, and a vignette darkens the corners.
Blur a copy heavily and draw thin white lines along its levels of equal brightness, one pixel wide whatever the slope.
Find the centre of everything that stands out from the mean tone, and draw a circle and a ticked rule from it.
Add grain, a few scratches and dust, then set the sentence small with wide letter spacing.
history: The essay film is older than the internet: Hans Richter described the form in 1940, and Chris Marker’s Sans Soleil (1983) is its best-known example. On video platforms in the 2010s the video essay became a genre of its own, often one voice over spare black-and-white visuals. The thin white diagram lines borrow from technical drawing and from the conceptual art of the 1960s, where a line and a caption could be the whole work.
uses: Slides that carry one idea each
terms: A line that joins points of equal value, here equal brightness.
A gradual darkening toward the corners of a picture.
Extra room set between the letters of a word.
paragraphs: The picture is reduced to brightness, stretched so that its darkest and lightest 2% clip, and then sunk. A smoothstep between two limits set by the “depth of the blacks” slider decides which greys survive: everything below the lower limit becomes black. The result is raised to the power 1.2 and scaled to 88%, so nothing in the frame is quite white, and a vignette takes away up to 55% more toward the corners. Grain is the sum of a per-pixel hash and a smoother value noise; a few vertical scratches and rare dust specks are drawn from the same seed.

The white contours are lines of equal brightness on a copy of the picture blurred twice with a box of radius 16 pixels. For each level, the distance from a pixel to the contour is estimated as the difference in brightness divided by the local slope, and the line is drawn where that distance is under about a pixel. Dividing by the slope is what keeps the line the same width on a gentle gradient and on a sharp edge. The circle is centred on the average position of everything that differs from the picture’s mean tone, each place weighted by the square of that difference.

equations.note: Tone: L is the stretched brightness, S the smoothstep and c the “depth of the blacks” slider (0 to 1).
Distance d to the contour at level ℓ on the blurred brightness L_w, and the opacity of a line of width w.

equations.tex: \mathbf c=\frac{\sum_i w_i\,\mathbf x_i}{\sum_i w_i},\qquad w_i=\big(L_{w,i}-\bar L\big)^{2}
equations.note: Centre of the circle: the weighted mean position of what stands out from the mean tone.

presets.text: One contour and deep blacks leave almost nothing but the line.
A warm tone and heavy grain look like an old print.
Turn the circle off and keep three contours for a map of the picture.
